planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; best where high-elevation nights stay cool but hard winter freezes are rare.

directions: Andean blueberry is a wild Ericaceae shrub of the high-elevation paramo and cloud-forest edges of Ecuador, Colombia, and Venezuela, where cool nights and warm days produce small, intensely tart-sweet blue-black berries traditionally used in the Ecuadorian colada morada drink. Its habit ranges from a low, spreading subshrub to an upright bush several feet tall depending on exposure, and while it fruits most heavily in open sun, plants tolerate light shade at forest margins. Grow in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil and expect two to three years of establishment before significant fruiting begins, much like other Vaccinium species. Because the species evolved under near-constant mild temperatures punctuated by nightly frost rather than prolonged winter cold, protect it from sustained hard freezes in cultivation.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or container stock in spring in acidic, moist, well-drained soil with some overhead canopy, mimicking its native forest-margin habitat.

directions: Agraz, also called Colombian mountain blueberry, grows wild on forested Andean slopes between roughly 7,200 and 11,000 feet, where local harvesters gather it from semi-wild stands rather than true plantations. Older plants develop long, sprawling, almost vine-like woody stems that can be layered for propagation, a habit distinct from the compact North American blueberries already in this database. Site it in acidic, consistently moist, well-drained soil with some overhead canopy, since in its native range it grows along forest margins and in partially shaded understory gaps. In favorable climates a single planting can produce two harvests a year, yielding small, dark purple berries valued fresh and in traditional Colombian preserves.
sources: Universidad Nacional de Colombia — Agronomia Colombiana journal

planting.note: Plant rooted tip cuttings in spring against a trellis or wire support in rich, well-drained soil; keep humidity and soil moisture consistently high.

directions: Mora de Castilla is the dominant commercial raspberry-blackberry of the tropical Andes, grown from Mexico south to Bolivia at elevations between roughly 5,000 and 10,000 feet, where daytime warmth and cool, humid nights suit it better than true lowland tropics. The long, arching, blue-green canes need a trellis or wire support to manage their vigorous growth and are usually propagated from tip cuttings or layered canes rather than seed. Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade and keep humidity and soil moisture consistently high; the plant is sensitive to hard frost and performs poorly where nights drop much below the mid-20s Fahrenheit. The glossy reddish-purple fruit is tart and juicy, widely juiced or made into preserves throughout its native range.

planting.note: Root layered cane sections in spring in humus-rich, consistently moist soil; give midday shade in warmer sites to mimic its cloud-forest origin.

directions: Mora silvestre is a wild highland blackberry gathered and increasingly cultivated in the cool cloud forests of Costa Rica and neighboring Central American highlands, typically above 8,500 feet where temperatures stay mild year-round. Its canes are notably bristly and can trail past 13 feet, rooting readily where cut sections are layered into moist soil, and plantings in the dappled light of forest-edge plots perform as well as those in open rows. Give it humus-rich, consistently moist soil and some midday shade in warmer sites, since the species is adapted to cool, cloud-shrouded conditions rather than intense tropical sun. The small, dark berries are notably high in anthocyanins and have long been a subject of Costa Rican food-science research into their antioxidant content.
sources: Instituto Tecnologico de Costa Rica research

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring; tolerates deep shade but fruits most heavily with several hours of direct sun daily. Can be locally weedy in mild, wet climates — site with containment in mind.

directions: Golden Himalayan raspberry is a robust, often semi-evergreen bramble native to humid forests from the western Himalayas across to southern China, where it grows equally well in deep shade beneath a forest canopy or in full sun along disturbed slopes and roadsides. The stout, bristly canes can reach up to 15 feet and bear clusters of small white flowers followed by golden-yellow, sweet fruit that ripens over a long season. Because it tolerates shade so readily, it is a useful bramble for the dim edges of a food-forest planting, though it fruits more heavily given several hours of direct sun. The species has become locally invasive in parts of Hawaii and other mild, wet climates, so gardeners in similar conditions should monitor and contain its spread by rhizome and seed.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; allow a decade for the mat to reach full spread.

directions: Prostrate barberry is a low, wide-spreading evergreen shrub from the gravelly, sun-exposed slopes of southern Chile and Argentina, forming a dense mat of small, narrow, holly-textured leaves on wiry, spiny stems under two feet tall. Small yellow spring flowers give way to round, blue-black berries with a tart, only mildly astringent flavor that can be eaten fresh in small quantities or cooked into jam, much like its larger Patagonian relative the calafate. It is extremely hardy and thrives in poor, lean, well-drained soil in full sun, tolerating exposure, drought, and cold far better than richer garden soils, and needs roughly a decade to reach full mature spread. Use it as a tough groundcover-scale edging plant on a slope or gravel garden where its sprawling habit and winter berry display can be appreciated.
